profile.beat: US small- and micro-cap healthcare — diagnostics, medtech/neuromodulation and clinical-stage biotech — held in a concentrated, margined book. He also runs a persistent top-down commentary on tech (QQQ, MAGS, SMH, IGV, software) that he mostly uses to explain why he refuses to own it.
profile.style: Fundamentals-first on valuation — he argues almost everything in EV/sales, EV/gross-profit and peak-sales-times-a-multiple terms — then overlays explicit technical triggers (9/21 EMA, 50d/200d, relative volume, support retests) for timing. He talks position sizing constantly: he names which slot a stock occupies in the book, posts his gross exposure, which is usually meaningfully above fully invested, and says outright when a name is his largest. Conviction language is blunt ('going much higher', 'too cheap', 'a great long from here', 'no brainer') but usually softened with 'imo', and he stops out fast on a broken level rather than averaging down ('Some people lean in during a drawdown | I lean away').
profile.cadence: Extremely high volume and reply-dominated: 813 of 1088 posts are replies. The default format is a one-line assertion or a back-and-forth in someone's mentions, punctuated by a handful of long-form essays that carry the real theses (7/15 valuation manifesto, 7/23 QQQ/MAGS/SMH/IGV market-structure breakdown, 8/17 CCCC pitch, 8/28 AI-demand-plateau piece). Recurring series: daily P&L and gross-exposure screenshots, 'X names, Y% long' portfolio updates, earnings-day reaction posts, and a weekly Discord workshop plug. A large share of the feed is off-topic (World Cup, food, Maui, his data-science masters, birthday).
profile.revisits: Constantly, in both directions. He tracks his own calls forward and takes explicit victory laps (2089843267261374683 and 2093433531460649173 on the tech-chop call; 2089041645048365292 on long MGNI / short TTD; 2090100161079112183 on XBI), and he also publishes reversals and losses: he downgraded QTRX to 'dead money' the morning after its print (2086805869162045885), listed his own mistakes including QTRX and STIM (2087201669750895025), flipped TEM from 'I cut the position today' (2077856355621429379) to 'a great long from here' (2079253033444376966) within three days on the PSNL deal, and posted that he had given back a lot of performance (2080746808524067209).
profile.caveats: He sells a paid Discord and says he stopped sharing his full portfolio on X (2090841452553412962), and ran a promo tied to the biotech rally (2091865611039097242) — so the public feed is a partial and self-selected view of what he actually holds. Performance is self-reported via screenshots only; he routinely runs margin well above fully invested, describes himself at times as 'levered long', and occasionally trades options, so his posted account returns are not comparable to unlevered stock returns. His largest winner in the window, PSNL, resolved through a takeover he explicitly called a disappointing price, not through his own target. Most picks are illiquid micro/small caps where a 40K-follower account can itself move price, and many names surface only as bare ticker lists in replies with no stated thesis. He is combative with critics, insults and blocks them, and several 'calls' he claims credit for (long MGNI / short TTD, NKTR, ABVX) originated before this window.

narrative: The window opens with him defensive: he cut exposure into a July momentum unwind, declared SMH had lost its uptrend, and re-built the book with smid-cap healthcare names he had watched for years. On 7/15 he published a valuation manifesto arguing that AI/robotics names like OUST and AMBA were priced for speculation while WGS, QTRX and STIM offered similar growth at a fraction of the multiple — the frame that governs everything after it. On 7/23 he extended that top-down into a specific call that tech would chop or go nowhere through year-end because MAGS capex kills the free-cash-flow multiple, software will not get its old premium back, and SMH has priced in the optimism; he repeated and defended this call all the way to 8/29. His single largest position, PSNL, was taken out by TEM on 7/20 at a price he called a 'huge buzzkill' — he booked the win, immediately rotated into TEM as the deal's winner, and spent the rest of the window arguing the PSNL deal opened a consolidation window across diagnostics (QTRX, WGS, XGN). Late July was his worst stretch — he admitted he was barely beating SPY — but he refused to touch tech and went to an all-healthcare book. From 8/4 onward the thesis paid: WGS, XGN and then STLN gapped up on earnings, he posted repeated new account highs, and he became loudly bullish on XBI, arguing after the MRK/MRNA cancer-vaccine news that biotech had more fuel and was not a place to short. The one clear miss he owned was QTRX: a name he had pitched since 7/15 as a re-rating candidate, held in size, and dumped the morning after a guide-down as 'dead money'. He closes the window trimming into an early-September pullback while arguing that falling yields are a tailwind for indebted small caps and long-duration biotech, and — after two months of being an AI bull who wouldn't own AI stocks — publishing his first fundamental doubt about AI demand growth itself.

picks.prospect: Expected PSNL to re-rate sharply as the credible number two to NTRA in MRD/liquid biopsy, and — once takeover chatter surfaced in mid-July — expected an outright sale of the business at a large premium, with Merck holding a right of first refusal against Tempus.
picks.risk_reward: He framed the upside as a takeout well above where it traded against a downside he barely discussed, arguing management's persistent stock selling and their willingness to entertain offers made a sale likely; his stated risk was not that the stock fell but that the board sold too cheap, which is exactly what he says happened.
picks.thesis: PSNL is the MRD engine behind TEM's clinical distribution and MRK's cancer-vaccine program, with both holding large equity stakes, yet it traded at a small fraction of NTRA's market cap. He used NTRA as the North Star for what a genomics duopoly participant should eventually be worth, and pointed to abnormal volume as evidence institutions were accumulating.
